subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: Evening on the farm. Sonali sat on the cot outside the house while her father, Pradeep, walked to the cowshed. Her eyes followed him the whole way. When he came back, he crouched beside her and pointed up. "Look, Sonali, parrot!" She turned her head and found the green bird in the mango tree. Then she looked back at his face, grinned, and stabbed her own little finger toward the branch.

qa.q: Where was the parrot?
qa.a: In the mango tree.

qa.q: What does Sonali's look back at Pradeep's face suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was interested in the parrot and wanted to share it with him, feeling safe and connected; it could also be that she was checking she had found the right thing.

qa.q: How could Pradeep keep building this shared looking?
qa.a: He could keep pointing at things around the farm, naming them, and waiting for her to point back.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Sonali points at the branch herself?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and close to her, seeing that she followed his point and shared it back. 😊

grounding: A toddler follows her father with her eyes and looks where he points, sharing attention on a bird.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
At the bus stop in Toronto, Dalia pointed across the road. "Leila, look, the big red bus!" For weeks Leila had rarely looked where Dalia pointed, and Dalia had written it down to ask about at the check-up.
Today Leila turned, found the bus and kept her eyes on it as it pulled in. Then she looked up at Dalia and said, "Bus."
Dalia smiled, and still kept the note in her bag for the doctor.

qa.q: What did Dalia point to across the road?
qa.a: The big red bus.

qa.q: What might Dalia have been feeling when Leila looked at the bus and said "Bus"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and happy, after weeks of worry that Leila rarely followed her pointing; she still seems a little unsure, since she kept the note.

qa.q: Was keeping the note for the doctor a good idea, and why?
qa.a: Yes, because a paediatrician can look at the whole picture, and asking costs nothing even if today went well.

qa.q: How does Leila seem to experience the moment?
qa.a: She seems interested in the bus and pleased to share it, looking up at Dalia to name it.

grounding: A mother notices her toddler starting to follow her point and still plans to raise the earlier worry with the doctor.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: I'm Imran, and on Sunday I took my little cousin Rafiq to watch the colony cricket match. Every time someone hit the ball, I pointed and shouted, "There it goes!" At first Rafiq just stared at my finger. By the third hit, his eyes flew off my hand and found the ball rolling toward the boundary. Then he looked straight back at me and laughed. I'm not sure he understood cricket. Maybe he just liked us looking together.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do by the third hit?
qa.a: His eyes flew off Imran's hand and found the ball rolling toward the boundary.

qa.q: What might Rafiq's laugh after looking back at Imran show?
qa.a: It likely shows delight at sharing the moment with Imran and trust in him, more than understanding the game; he may simply have enjoyed the ball moving.

qa.q: What small step could help Rafiq follow points more easily?
qa.a: Pointing at big, moving things and saying their name, as Imran did, then waiting for him to look back.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when Rafiq looks back at him?
qa.a: Imran feels included and amused, though unsure what Rafiq understood, and values the looking together.

grounding: A cousin sees a toddler move from staring at a pointing finger to following it and sharing attention on the ball.

subtype: Looking away when overwhelmed [Regulating]
passage:
At the birthday party in Bristol, Aunt Ada swooped down on Freya with a loud "BOO-BOO-BOO!" and wiggled her fingers near her tummy. Freya didn't cry. She turned her eyes to the wall and went quiet, fingers twisting her sock.
"Oh, she doesn't like me," Ada said.
Freya's dad shook his head. "Try softer." Ada sat back and hummed quietly. After a while, Freya's eyes came back to her face, and she smiled.

qa.q: What did Freya do with her fingers while looking at the wall?
qa.a: She twisted her sock.

qa.q: What was Freya likely feeling when she turned her eyes to the wall?
qa.a: She was likely overwhelmed by the loud game and was calming herself down, not rejecting Ada; her smile later shows she was still fond of her.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The game was too loud and close for Freya; sitting back and humming quietly lowered the intensity so she could look back.

qa.q: How does Ada see the look away at first?
qa.a: Ada feels hurt and takes it as rejection, until the softer approach shows Freya just needed a break.

grounding: A toddler looks away from a loud, intense game to calm down, and the adult lowers the intensity instead of taking it as rejection.

subtype: Looking away when overwhelmed [Regulating]
passage: I'm Zeenat, the neighbour, and I was at the naming party next door. Six relatives crowded round little Elizabeth at once, all cooing and clapping. She didn't cry. She just stared hard at the curtain, turning her head away each time someone leaned in. "She's shy of us," one aunt said, sounding hurt. Her mother asked everyone to step back and sit. A few minutes later, Elizabeth peeped out and reached for her grandmother. I wondered if she'd just needed quiet.

qa.q: How many relatives crowded round Elizabeth at once?
qa.a: Six relatives.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth's stare at the curtain have meant?
qa.a: It likely meant she felt overwhelmed by so many faces and noise and was giving herself a break; it may also have been some shyness, but she was not rejecting her family.

qa.q: Which choice of the mother's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking everyone to step back and sit lowered the crowding, so Elizabeth could calm down and reach for her grandmother.

qa.q: How does the aunt who spoke see Elizabeth's turning away?
qa.a: The aunt feels hurt and reads it as shyness or dislike, rather than a small child needing less noise.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler look away from a crowd of cooing relatives, a calming break rather than rejection.

subtype: Looking away when overwhelmed [Regulating]

Saturday: Tanvir flew Indu round the room like a plane, making loud engine noises. Indu turned her eyes away to the window. He kept going, louder. She burst into tears.
Tuesday: same game. When Indu looked away again, Tanvir slowed down and dropped his voice to a whisper. She looked back and smiled.
The next Sunday: when she looked away, Tanvir just held still and waited. Indu turned back, laughing, and flapped her arms for more.

qa.a: He flew her round the room like a plane, making loud engine noises.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling each time she looked away?
qa.a: She was feeling overwhelmed by the noise and movement and was taking a break to calm down; by Sunday her laughing return shows she was happy once the break was respected.

qa.q: What did Tanvir learn to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: He learned to slow down, whisper or wait when she looked away, which lowered the intensity so she could come back to the game.

qa.q: What would change if Tanvir had decided Indu disliked the game?
qa.a: He might have stopped playing it altogether, and they would have lost a game she actually enjoyed. 🙂

grounding: Over several days a father learns to read his toddler's looking away as a need for a calmer game, not rejection.

In their Mumbai flat, Rukmini was blowing up balloons for the evening puja, her cheeks swelling with every breath. Her little brother Zubin watched from the floor. Then he puffed his own cheeks out, his face going red, and held them there, eyes wide.
"Let it out!" Rukmini laughed. He did, with a loud "pah!" Her balloon finally grew fat and round. Zubin's cheeks rose into a smile so big his eyes nearly disappeared.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]

She turned her face into my shirt. Her Amma laughed and said, "Too strong, na?" and walked us to the fruit side. I couldn't tell if she hated the smell or was just startled by it. Near the bananas she looked up again.

qa.q: Which stall made Lakshmi crinkle her nose?
qa.a: The dried-fish stall.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi's wrinkled nose and lifted lip suggest she felt?
qa.a: Most likely disgust at the strong smell; turning into Deepak's shirt might also mean she was startled or overwhelmed.

qa.a: She named it ("Too strong, na?") and moved them to the fruit side, without making Lakshmi stay near the smell.

qa.a: Deepak notices the reaction clearly but isn't sure whether it was dislike or surprise.

Day five: a little spinach sat next to the rice on the plate. Anirban poked it, sniffed his finger, and his nose crinkled only a bit.
Day twelve: he took two bites of the green rice himself. "Okay," he announced.

qa.q: What did Omkar give Anirban on day one after he pushed the spoon away?

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]

The garbage van rumbled into the Delhi colony lane just as Baljeet was toddling out with his father. Baljeet stopped, screwed up his nose and squeezed his mouth tight. He pulled at his father's hand, backwards.
Yusuf, who lived on the ground floor, was watering his plants. He wrinkled his own nose and laughed. "Same, beta. Very smelly!"
Baljeet stared at him, then wrinkled his nose again, and this time he giggled.

qa.a: He felt disgusted by the smell of the garbage van and wanted to get away from it; his giggle later suggests the shared joke made him feel better.

qa.a: He likely understands it as a simple reaction to a bad smell and is glad the neighbour made it light.

subtype: Puckering and lip stretching [Expressing]

qa.a: He would probably feel touched and a little reluctant to catch the bus.

Mei ran straight back into the spray, squealing again, lips stretched in a grin, and looked back to see if Amara was watching.
Amara relaxed and clapped. "Again? Go on!"

qa.a: Watching what Mei did next, running back and looking round to share it, instead of judging the squeal alone.

subtype: Puckering and lip stretching [Expressing]

At the small-town bus stand, Karthik's orange ice lolly slid off its stick and landed in the dust. He stared at it. His lower lip turned down, then began to quiver.
His grandfather, Raghav, did not say "Don't cry." He lifted Karthik onto his knee and spoke low. "Oh, it fell. That's sad." Karthik's lip shook, he cried a little into Thatha's shirt, and then he leaned there, breathing slowly.

qa.q: Where did Karthik's ice lolly land?
qa.a: In the dust at the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as his lip quivered?
qa.a: He was feeling sad and disappointed at losing his lolly; the quiver shows tears were coming.

qa.a: He would probably feel tender and glad that his closeness is calming Karthik.

In the shopping centre toilets in Melbourne, the hand dryer roared on right beside Rania. She pressed back against Tuan's legs. Her bottom lip pushed out and trembled.
Tuan crouched, covered her ears with his warm hands and put his face close to hers. "Loud, loud. I've got you," he said softly. Her lip stopped shaking after a moment. He carried her out to the quiet corridor before drying her hands on his shirt.

qa.q: How did Tuan dry Rania's hands?
qa.a: On his shirt, out in the quiet corridor.

qa.q: What does Rania's trembling lip suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and frightened by the sudden roar of the hand dryer, close to crying.

qa.q: Which of Tuan's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Covering her ears, speaking softly close to her face and taking her somewhere quiet worked, because it lowered the noise and gave her comfort.

qa.q: What would change if Tuan had told Rania the dryer was nothing to be scared of?
qa.a: Her fear would be brushed aside, and she might have cried harder instead of calming.

A visiting aunty laughed. "Close your mouth, Avni, don't gape. Looks so rude."
Himani, her mother, knelt beside her. "She's not rude, she's amazed." She pointed. "Up goes the crane." Avni followed her finger, mouth still open, and whispered, "Up."

qa.a: Himani sees amazement, while the aunty sees bad manners.
